1: Neither Burton & Goodspeed nor Huck opens with a prologue section — both are synoptic-only harmonies and have no John column at all. Setting Mark 1:1, Matthew 1:1, Luke 1:1–4 and John 1:1–18 side by side as four different answers to the question "how do you begin?" is this synopsis's own arrangement, and one of the most useful pages here.
6: The genealogy is printed twice in this synopsis — here at its Matthean position and again at ¶19 where Luke places it. Burton & Goodspeed print it once. Printing it twice costs a little redundancy and buys the ability to read each writer's sequence without interruption.
19: The second printing of the genealogy, at Luke's position after the baptism. See ¶6.
25: John's temple cleansing is placed here, early, where John places it, with the synoptic parallels shown alongside for comparison. The synoptic cleansing is printed again at ¶273 in Holy Week. Neither harmony this was checked against includes John, so the double placement is this synopsis's judgment, not an inherited one. See the Chronology & context note.
50: Matthew's Sermon on the Mount (¶50–76) and Luke's Sermon on the Plain (¶77–83) are given separate sections here, each read straight through, with the cross-parallels shown in the columns. Huck instead runs Luke's sermon as a parallel column against Matthew's. Both arrangements are defensible; this one lets a reader hear each sermon as its author composed it.
84: Sections 8 and 5 both carry material from Matthew 8–9 and Mark 1–3. Matthew groups by theme where Mark runs chronologically, so the same episodes appear at two points in any synopsis that tries to preserve both sequences. The repeated pericopes are marked "(Matthew's Order)" or "(Mark's Order)" so it is clear which sequence you are reading.
114: The anointing appears four times in this synopsis (¶114, ¶267, ¶306, and Luke's separate scene). Luke 7:36–50 is almost certainly a different event — a different city, a different host's motive, a different response — and is shown here for comparison, not as a parallel. See the Chronology & context notes at ¶267 and ¶306.
294: Mark and Luke give different conclusions to the Olivet discourse, so both are printed (¶294 Mark, ¶295 Luke) rather than merged. The Lukan verses in the Markan row are the nearest sayings-parallels, not the same text.
309: The sayings-parallels printed against John 13:16 are Matthew 10:24 and Luke 6:40. The source transcription read "Luke 6.4", which is a slip for 6:40; corrected here, and recorded so the correction is visible.
312: This row duplicates ¶310 — same episode, same references. It was carried in the source transcription and is kept so the section numbering stays stable, but there is nothing here that ¶310 does not already show. Treat it as a placeholder.
361: 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 is Paul's list of resurrection appearances, the earliest such list in the New Testament and older than any gospel. It is printed here as a citation for comparison, not as a gospel passage; the source transcription placed it in the Mark column, which is an error of the spreadsheet rather than a claim about Mark.
362: The Shorter Ending of Mark has no verse numbers: it is a floating paragraph that a handful of witnesses (L, Ψ, 083, 099, 274 margin, 579, and the Old Latin k) place after Mark 16:8 — some instead of the Longer Ending, some before it. It is absent from every translation carried here, which is why no verse text loads in this row. Mark 16:1–8 is not the shorter ending; that is ¶352.
363: Mark 16:9–20, the Longer Ending, is absent from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; Eusebius reports that many copies known to him did so, and Jerome echoes this report (a statement that appears closely dependent on Eusebius rather than an independent witness). It is nonetheless ancient, quoted by Irenaeus in the second century, widely transmitted, and it stands in the King James Version. Read it here as what it is: a very early conclusion, not demonstrably Mark's own.
_about: Editorial notes on this synopsis: where the divisions are contested, where a reference is doubtful, and where this arrangement differs from the public-domain harmonies it was checked against (Burton & Goodspeed 1920; Huck 1892).
